A spasm is a sudden, involuntary contraction — a tight, forceful squeezing — of a muscle or group of muscles that happens on its own, without you choosing or wanting it to happen. Three words define every spasm: sudden, involuntary, and contraction. If any of these three qualities is missing, it's probably not a spasm.

Sudden means it happens without warning. You don't feel it slowly building up the way tiredness does. It arrives abruptly, almost like a shock.

Involuntary means you are not in control of it. Your brain didn't send a deliberate signal telling the muscle to tighten. Your body did it all on its own, the same way your eye blinks automatically when something flies toward your face. You can't just "will" a spasm to stop.

Contraction means the muscle shortens and tightens, rather than relaxing or stretching. Think of how your fist clenches when you squeeze it hard — that's a contraction. In a spasm, the muscle does that, but without your permission.
What a spasm feels like and how long it lasts

A spasm is usually brief — it can last anywhere from a split second to a few minutes. Some spasms are mild and barely noticeable, like the tiny flutter you sometimes feel under your eyelid. Others are intense and very painful, like the agonizing tightening in your calf muscle in the middle of the night that makes you want to cry out. The severity really depends on which muscle is spasming and why.

After a spasm, the muscle usually returns to normal on its own. However, if spasms keep happening one after another in rapid succession, that pattern is called clonic spasms, while a single prolonged, sustained squeeze is called a tonic spasm — but in everyday language, both are simply called spasms.

Most people think of spasms only in terms of the muscles you can feel — your back, your legs, your neck. But the word spasm applies to any muscle in the body, including muscles inside your organs and blood vessels, which you normally can't feel at all.

Your airways (the tubes that carry air into your lungs) are lined with muscle. When those muscles spasm, the airways suddenly narrow, making it hard to breathe. This is exactly what happens during an asthma attack and is called a bronchospasm. It's still a spasm — sudden, involuntary, and a contraction — just happening somewhere you can't see or touch.

Similarly, the walls of your arteries (blood vessels) contain muscle. When those spasm, the artery suddenly tightens and blood flow through it drops. A coronary artery spasm — a spasm in the arteries of the heart — can actually cause chest pain, and in severe cases, even a heart attack. This shows how the same basic concept (sudden involuntary muscle tightening) plays out in very different and sometimes dangerous ways depending on location.

The intestines, the esophagus, the bladder — all of these hollow organs contain muscle, and all of them can spasm. An intestinal spasm produces the cramping, griping pain you might feel during a stomach upset.
How spasm differs from similar words

A cramp is essentially a sustained, painful spasm — it's a spasm that holds on for a while and hurts a great deal. The two words are often used interchangeably in everyday speech, and that's fine, but technically a cramp is a specific type of spasm.

A twitch is a very small, brief, mild involuntary movement — usually just a tiny flicker visible under the skin. A spasm is generally stronger and more forceful than a twitch, though a very mild spasm might look like a twitch.

A tremor is a rhythmic, repetitive shaking that keeps going — like the shaking hands seen in Parkinson's disease. A spasm is not rhythmic or repetitive in that way; it's a single event (or a burst of events), not a continuous tremor.

A convulsion or seizure involves widespread, uncontrolled electrical activity in the brain causing many muscles to spasm simultaneously and violently across the whole body. So a convulsion is, in a sense, made up of many spasms happening together, but the word "convulsion" implies a much larger, more dramatic, whole-body event driven by the brain misfiring.

In everyday language, the word spasm is also used figuratively — to describe any sudden, brief, and somewhat uncontrolled burst of a feeling or activity. Just as a muscle spasm is a sudden, short-lived, uncontrolled physical event, a "spasm" of emotion is a sudden, short-lived, uncontrolled emotional event.

For example: "He felt a spasm of guilt when he saw her crying." This means a sudden, sharp, brief wave of guilt hit him involuntarily — he didn't plan to feel it, it just arrived and then passed, much like a muscle spasm does.

Other examples of this figurative use: a spasm of laughter, a spasm of rage, a spasm of panic, a spasm of activity (meaning a sudden short burst of doing a lot). The common thread is always the same: sudden, uncontrolled, and brief.
Common phrases and collocations you'll encounter

You'll often see spasm used with these words: muscle spasm, back spasm, neck spasm, leg spasm, stomach spasm, bronchial spasm, arterial spasm, infantile spasms (a specific type of epileptic seizure in babies), and in spasm (e.g., "her back was in spasm," meaning the muscle was locked in a sustained contraction).

A spasm is a sudden, involuntary, forceful tightening of a muscle — anywhere in the body — that you didn't choose and can't easily control, and the word can also be used figuratively to describe any sudden, brief, uncontrolled burst of emotion or activity.
